Area Under Curves — JEE Main revision guide

Area is built by adding thin strips. The main work is choosing the right strips and their endpoints. A correct integral starts with a correct picture.

Study priority: draw intersections, decide top/bottom or right/left, split at changes, use symmetry, and recognise simple geometric areas. This is a teaching priority, not a measured formula-frequency rank.

Scope and difficulties before studying

The official integration unit includes finding areas bounded by simple curves in standard forms. We teach the required integration, graph and elementary geometry tools here without assuming later conics chapters have already been revised.

The 252525 intended source answers agree with independent setups. Three wording points need care:

  • Q14 asks for the finite closed region under the lower of tangent and cotangent, with the axis below.
  • In Q21 use the positive closed region from 111 to 222, avoiding the hyperbola's pole at 000.
  • Q22's first intersection means the first positive one after their shared point at the origin.

Concept C01 — What a strip of area means

An area counts the amount of flat space inside a boundary. It is nonnegative and has square units.

Take a very thin vertical rectangle. Its width is dxdxdx and height is top minus bottom:

dA=[ytop(x)−ybottom(x)] dx.dA=[y_{\rm top}(x)-y_{\rm bottom}(x)]\,dx.dA=[ytop​(x)−ybottom​(x)]dx.

Adding all strips gives the exact area as the widths shrink:

A=∫ab[ytop(x)−ybottom(x)]dx.\boxed{A=\int_a^b[y_{\rm top}(x)-y_{\rm bottom}(x)]dx}.A=∫ab​[ytop​(x)−ybottom​(x)]dx​.

This needs a<ba<ba<b and the same top/bottom ordering on the whole piece. The height is a difference of coordinates, not necessarily the distance of the top curve from the axis.

For a region between y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) and the axis:

A=∫ab∣f(x)∣dx.\boxed{A=\int_a^b|f(x)|dx}.A=∫ab​∣f(x)∣dx​.

For two curves whose order can switch:

A=∫ab∣f(x)−g(x)∣dx,\boxed{A=\int_a^b|f(x)-g(x)|dx},A=∫ab​∣f(x)−g(x)∣dx​,

with appropriate splitting. The modulus belongs inside the integral; taking a modulus only after signed areas cancel cannot recover the lost area.

Concept C02 — Turn the strip sideways when that is simpler

A horizontal strip has thickness dydydy. Its length is right boundary minus left boundary:

A=∫cd[xright(y)−xleft(y)]dy.\boxed{A=\int_c^d[x_{\rm right}(y)-x_{\rm left}(y)]dy}.A=∫cd​[xright​(y)−xleft​(y)]dy​.

Important for JEE Main: choose the direction that needs fewer pieces and simpler boundary formulas.

For y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x and y=xy=xy=x, a vertical strip uses 2x−x2\sqrt x-x2x​−x. A horizontal strip uses y−y2/4y-y^2/4y−y2/4. Both are valid; the horizontal version avoids a square root.

For x=y2x=y^2x=y2 and x=3−2y2x=3-2y^2x=3−2y2, the equations already give left/right positions. Solving each for yyy would create upper and lower branches unnecessarily.

Do not write top minus bottom and then integrate in dydydy. The strip direction, boundary coordinates and differential must agree.

Concept C03 — Build the closed boundary before integrating

“Bounded” means the curves or lines form a closed fence around a finite region.

  1. Find intersections using the original equations and domains.
  2. Include every stated boundary: an axis or x=ax=ax=a can close a region.
  3. Mark a point between consecutive intersections to decide the order.
  4. Split if the boundary curve or its expression changes.

For y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x, x≥0x\ge0x≥0. Writing y=2xy=2\sqrt xy=2x​ chooses only the upper branch; the lower branch is −2x-2\sqrt x−2x​. Which one belongs to the closed region must come from the picture.

For x=x3\sqrt x=x^3x​=x3, require x≥0x\ge0x≥0 first. Then x=0x=0x=0 or x=1x=1x=1; squaring without checking a domain can create unwanted candidates.

A useful midpoint test: if f−gf-gf−g is continuous and has no zero inside the piece, its sign cannot change there. One test point decides the order on that piece. The picture suggests the order; this sign argument confirms it.

Concept C04 — Signed integral versus ordinary area

The integral ∫f\int f∫f adds above-axis strips and subtracts below-axis strips. Area adds their positive sizes.

For a full sine cycle:

∫02πsin⁡x dx=0,∫02π∣sin⁡x∣dx=4.\int_0^{2\pi}\sin x\,dx=0,\qquad \int_0^{2\pi}|\sin x|dx=4.∫02π​sinxdx=0,∫02π​∣sinx∣dx=4.

For ln⁡x\ln xlnx, the zero is x=1x=1x=1. Thus a region spanning that input needs

A=−∫a1ln⁡x dx+∫1bln⁡x dx(0<a<1<b).A=-\int_a^1\ln x\,dx+\int_1^b\ln x\,dx \quad(0<a<1<b).A=−∫a1​lnxdx+∫1b​lnxdx(0<a<1<b).

For y=x∣x∣y=x|x|y=x∣x∣, y=−x2y=-x^2y=−x2 on the negative side and y=x2y=x^2y=x2 on the positive side. Its absolute height is x2x^2x2 on both sides. Simplifying that height first can save casework.

Concept C05 — Symmetry saves work; corners still need splitting

If the whole region mirrors across the yyy-axis:

A=2∫0a(top−bottom)dx.A=2\int_0^a(\text{top}-\text{bottom})dx.A=2∫0a​(top−bottom)dx.

If it mirrors across both axes, four times the first-quadrant area may be easier.

Use

∣x∣={−x,x<0,x,x≥0,∣x−1∣={1−x,x<1,x−1,x≥1.|x|=\begin{cases}-x,&x<0,\\x,&x\ge0,\end{cases} \qquad |x-1|=\begin{cases}1-x,&x<1,\\x-1,&x\ge1.\end{cases}∣x∣={−x,x,​x<0,x≥0,​∣x−1∣={1−x,x−1,​x<1,x≥1.​

For several moduli, collect all their corner inputs and split at each one. Do not assume symmetry only because one boundary is even; the other boundary and any cutting lines must also preserve the region.

Translations move a region without changing its area. Rotations also preserve area and can reveal an ordinary rectangle in a tilted picture, as in Q25.

Concept C07 — Useful primitives and trig clues

Use the earlier integration chapter, including conditions:

∫xndx=xn+1n+1+C(n≠−1),∫ln⁡x dx=xln⁡x−x+C(x>0),∫dxx=ln⁡∣x∣+C,∫ekxdx=ekxk+C (k≠0),∫sin⁡x dx=−cos⁡x+C,∫cos⁡x dx=sin⁡x+C,∫tan⁡x dx=−ln⁡∣cos⁡x∣+C,∫cot⁡x dx=ln⁡∣sin⁡x∣+C.\begin{aligned} \int x^n dx&=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\quad(n\ne-1),\\ \int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x-x+C\quad(x>0),\\ \int\frac{dx}x&=\ln|x|+C,\qquad \int e^{kx}dx=\frac{e^{kx}}k+C\ (k\ne0),\\ \int\sin x\,dx&=-\cos x+C,\quad \int\cos x\,dx=\sin x+C,\\ \int\tan x\,dx&=-\ln|\cos x|+C,\quad \int\cot x\,dx=\ln|\sin x|+C. \end{aligned}∫xndx∫lnxdx∫xdx​∫sinxdx∫tanxdx​=n+1xn+1​+C(n=−1),=xlnx−x+C(x>0),=ln∣x∣+C,∫ekxdx=kekx​+C (k=0),=−cosx+C,∫cosxdx=sinx+C,=−ln∣cosx∣+C,∫cotxdx=ln∣sinx∣+C.​

For circle boundaries, R>0R>0R>0:

∫R2−x2dx=12[xR2−x2+R2sin⁡−1xR]+C\int\sqrt{R^2-x^2}dx =\frac12\left[x\sqrt{R^2-x^2}+R^2\sin^{-1}\frac xR\right]+C∫R2−x2​dx=21​[xR2−x2​+R2sin−1Rx​]+C

on the interior ∣x∣<R|x|<R∣x∣<R, extending to finite endpoints by a limit.

Trig intersections: sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x\sin2x=2\sin x\cos xsin2x=2sinxcosx. In a positive interval, cancelling sin⁡x\sin xsinx is valid only after recording its zero endpoints. Also tan⁡x=cot⁡x\tan x=\cot xtanx=cotx in (0,π/2)(0,\pi/2)(0,π/2) gives tan⁡x=1\tan x=1tanx=1, hence x=π/4x=\pi/4x=π/4.

Use radians for every integral formula involving angles. A finite plot supports the region choice; the intersection equations establish the exact endpoints.

Concept C08 — A region written as inequalities

An inequality such as x2≤y≤6−∣x∣x^2\le y\le6-|x|x2≤y≤6−∣x∣ says:

  • the point must be above y=x2y=x^2y=x2;
  • it must also be below y=6−∣x∣y=6-|x|y=6−∣x∣.

There is a vertical strip only where bottom ≤\le≤ top. Solve that condition to get the horizontal range.

Likewise, “inside x2+y2≤2x^2+y^2\le2x2+y2≤2 and above y=x2y=x^2y=x2” is an intersection of two conditions. The parabola is nonnegative, so only the upper circle boundary can be the top of this particular region.

Common mistake: the area of the whole disc minus the entire area “under the parabola” over an arbitrary interval is not automatically the requested region. First identify the actual common boundaries.

Concept C09 — A parabola-line gap has a useful cubic-width pattern

Important for JEE Main. If the positive gap between two boundaries is

h(x)=K(x−a)(b−x),K>0,a≤x≤b,h(x)=K(x-a)(b-x),\quad K>0,\quad a\le x\le b,h(x)=K(x−a)(b−x),K>0,a≤x≤b,

then, with L=b−aL=b-aL=b−a and u=(x−a)/Lu=(x-a)/Lu=(x−a)/L,

A=KL3∫01u(1−u)du=K(b−a)36.A=KL^3\int_0^1u(1-u)du =\boxed{\frac{K(b-a)^3}6}.A=KL3∫01​u(1−u)du=6K(b−a)3​​.

The extra width factor comes from dx=L dudx=L\,dudx=Ldu; height already contains L2L^2L2. This explains why halving the width does not usually halve area.

For 2x+3−x2=(x+1)(3−x)2x+3-x^2=(x+1)(3-x)2x+3−x2=(x+1)(3−x), K=1K=1K=1 and width is 444, so A=43/6A=4^3/6A=43/6. Learn the factorisation and the condition before using the shortcut.

For an equal-area cut, first find the whole area, then set the chosen piece to half. In Q15, the cap between the line and parabola has width 1−m1-m1−m and area (1−m)3/6(1-m)^3/6(1−m)3/6. It is only one of the two pieces of the original region.

Concept C10 — Circular segments and overlapping discs

A segment is the cap between a chord and its circular arc. It is a sector minus a triangle.

For a circle of radius RRR and a chord at distance ddd from the centre, 0≤d≤R0\le d\le R0≤d≤R, set the half-angle α=cos⁡−1(d/R)\alpha=\cos^{-1}(d/R)α=cos−1(d/R). The full sector angle is 2α2\alpha2α.

Asmaller cap=R2cos⁡−1dR−dR2−d2.\boxed{A_{\rm smaller\ cap} =R^2\cos^{-1}\frac dR-d\sqrt{R^2-d^2}}.Asmaller cap​=R2cos−1Rd​−dR2−d2​​.

Why the second term? The chord has length 2R2−d22\sqrt{R^2-d^2}2R2−d2​, so the triangle area is half that base times height ddd.

For equal-radius overlapping discs, draw their common chord. The lens is two segments:

Alens=2R2cos⁡−1D2R−D24R2−D2,0≤D≤2R,A_{\rm lens} =2R^2\cos^{-1}\frac D{2R} -\frac D2\sqrt{4R^2-D^2}, \quad0\le D\le2R,Alens​=2R2cos−12RD​−2D​4R2−D2​,0≤D≤2R,

where DDD is the centre separation. For D>2RD>2RD>2R, the common area is zero. This formula is a convenient consequence of the picture, not a substitute for drawing it.

An integral route is equally valid: use the smaller upper height and larger lower height at each input, splitting where the controlling circle changes. The geometry route often gives fewer algebra steps.

Concept C11 — Indirect curves, parameter curves and geometric alternatives

An implicit equation can often be rewritten as x=g(y)x=g(y)x=g(y) more simply than y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x). Use horizontal strips instead of forcing square roots and branches.

For a parametrized curve x=x(t),y=y(t)x=x(t),y=y(t)x=x(t),y=y(t) describing a nonnegative upper boundary with monotone increasing xxx,

A=∫y(t)x′(t) dtA=\int y(t)x'(t)\,dtA=∫y(t)x′(t)dt

over the corresponding parameter range. This is just dx=x′(t)dtdx=x'(t)dtdx=x′(t)dt in the strip formula. If the direction reverses, handle orientation and split into suitable pieces; a signed line integral is not automatically total geometric area.

Another useful view: before calculating, ask whether the enclosed region is a triangle, rectangle, diamond or sector in a different orientation. In Q25, four straight sides of slopes +1,−1+1,-1+1,−1 form a rotated rectangle. Adjacent side lengths give the area directly.

Concept C12 — Route choice and quick checks

Visible clue What to do before calculating
Equations give xxx in terms of yyy Try horizontal strips
A curve crosses the axis Split signed contributions into positive areas
Absolute values Mark every inside-zero point and use the correct signs
Symmetry of the whole region Integrate one half or one quarter
Disc and line Sector minus triangle, or the circle-root primitive
Equal-area condition Express one piece and equate to half the total
Two inequalities Identify the top and bottom simultaneously
Parabola minus line Factor the quadratic gap; check the cubic-width shortcut

Size checks: area must be nonnegative; a contained region cannot exceed its containing rectangle/disc. A common area cannot exceed either disc. If all coordinates are multiplied by sss, area multiplies by s2s^2s2. If only horizontal lengths multiply by aaa and vertical lengths by bbb, area multiplies by ∣ab∣|ab|∣ab∣.

Before submitting: draw; find exact intersections; choose strip direction; identify the actual closed region; split at sign/boundary changes; check units; then answer the quantity asked, including any multiplier such as 3A3A3A or kkk.

Worked solutions to the 25 PDF questions

Read the question first. Notice the pattern, choose a route, then calculate. Alternative methods below are fully visible.

Question 1 — Choose horizontal strips to avoid a square root

PDF page 71 | MCQ | Notes: C01,C02,C03

The area of the region bounded by the parabola y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x and the line y=xy=xy=x is

  • (a) 163\dfrac{16}3316​ sq. units
  • (b) 43\dfrac4334​ sq. units
  • (c) 83\dfrac8338​ sq. units
  • (d) 323\dfrac{32}3332​ sq. units

First close the fence. Substitute y=xy=xy=x into y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x: x2=4xx^2=4xx2=4x, so the intersections are (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) and (4,4)(4,4)(4,4).

Horizontal strips are simpler here. At a fixed height yyy, the parabola is at x=y2/4x=y^2/4x=y2/4 and the line at x=yx=yx=y. On 0<y<40<y<40<y<4, the line is to the right.

A=∫04(y−y24)dy=[y22−y312]04=8−163=83(c).A=\int_0^4\left(y-\frac{y^2}4\right)dy =\left[\frac{y^2}2-\frac{y^3}{12}\right]_0^4 =8-\frac{16}3=\boxed{\frac83}\quad\text{(c)}.A=∫04​(y−4y2​)dy=[2y2​−12y3​]04​=8−316​=38​​(c).

Another possible approach — vertical strips.

The upper branch is y=2xy=2\sqrt xy=2x​ and the lower curve is y=xy=xy=x: A=∫04(2x−x)dx=32/3−8=8/3A=\int_0^4(2\sqrt x-x)dx=32/3-8=8/3A=∫04​(2x​−x)dx=32/3−8=8/3. Both routes work; the horizontal one avoids the square root. The negative parabola branch forms no second closed region with this line.

Question 2 — An even region lets us use only its right half

PDF page 71 | MCQ | Notes: C03,C05

The area of the region bounded by y=x2y=x^2y=x2 and y=2−∣x∣y=2-|x|y=2−∣x∣ is

  • (a) 73\dfrac7337​ sq. units
  • (b) 53\dfrac5335​ sq. units
  • (c) 143\dfrac{14}3314​ sq. units
  • (d) 83\dfrac8338​ sq. units

Both boundaries are even, so the full region mirrors across the yyy-axis. On the right, ∣x∣=x|x|=x∣x∣=x. Intersections satisfy x2=2−xx^2=2-xx2=2−x, giving x=1x=1x=1 as the nonnegative root. The other intersection is its mirror at −1-1−1.

A=2∫01(2−x−x2)dx=2(2−12−13)=73(a).A=2\int_0^1(2-x-x^2)dx =2\left(2-\frac12-\frac13\right) =\boxed{\frac73}\quad\text{(a)}.A=2∫01​(2−x−x2)dx=2(2−21​−31​)=37​​(a).

Check the region: at x=0x=0x=0 the top is 222 and bottom 000, so the chosen order is correct. The total fits inside a rectangle of width 222 and height 222.

Question 3 — Keep the two different parabola equations distinct

PDF page 71 | Numerical value | Notes: C02,C03

If AAA is the area bounded by the parabolas y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x and x2=4yx^2=4yx2=4y, then 3A=3A=3A= ____ sq. units.

The two equations describe different parabolas. Their common points are (0,0),(4,4)(0,0),(4,4)(0,0),(4,4). For example, substituting y=x2/4y=x^2/4y=x2/4 into y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x gives x=0x=0x=0 or x3=64x^3=64x3=64.

A=∫04(2x−x24)dx=323−163=163.A=\int_0^4\left(2\sqrt x-\frac{x^2}4\right)dx =\frac{32}3-\frac{16}3=\frac{16}3.A=∫04​(2x​−4x2​)dx=332​−316​=316​.

The requested quantity is 3A=16\boxed{3A=16}3A=16​.

Another possible view: the region is unchanged when x,yx,yx,y are swapped. Horizontal strips therefore give ∫04(2y−y2/4)dy\int_0^4(2\sqrt y-y^2/4)dy∫04​(2y​−y2/4)dy, the same calculation with the strip turned sideways.

Question 4 — The y-axis closes the region at x zero

PDF page 71 | MCQ | Notes: C03,C07

The area of the region bounded by y=sin⁡xy=\sin xy=sinx, y=cos⁡xy=\cos xy=cosx and the yyy-axis, lying in the first quadrant, is

  • (a) 2+1\sqrt2+12​+1
  • (b) 22−22\sqrt2-222​−2
  • (c) 1−121-\dfrac1{\sqrt2}1−2​1​
  • (d) 2−1\sqrt2-12​−1

The yyy-axis means x=0x=0x=0, so it closes the left edge. The curves first meet in the first quadrant where sin⁡x=cos⁡x\sin x=\cos xsinx=cosx, giving x=π/4x=\pi/4x=π/4.

The inequality already names the bottom and top. A strip starts at y=x2y=x^2y=x2 and ends at y=6−∣x∣y=6-|x|y=6−∣x∣. It exists only when x2≤6−∣x∣x^2\le6-|x|x2≤6−∣x∣.

Set u=∣x∣≥0u=|x|\ge0u=∣x∣≥0. The condition is u2+u−6≤0u^2+u-6\le0u2+u−6≤0, so 0≤u≤20\le u\le20≤u≤2, or −2≤x≤2-2\le x\le2−2≤x≤2.

By symmetry,

A=2∫02(6−x−x2)dx=2(12−2−83)=443.A=2\int_0^2(6-x-x^2)dx =2\left(12-2-\frac83\right)=\frac{44}3.A=2∫02​(6−x−x2)dx=2(12−2−38​)=344​.

The requested result is 3A=44\boxed{3A=44}3A=44​.

Question 25 — Two V-shaped graphs also form a rotated rectangle

PDF page 73 | MCQ | Notes: C05,C11

The area of the region bounded by y=∣x−1∣y=|x-1|y=∣x−1∣ and y=3−∣x∣y=3-|x|y=3−∣x∣ is

  • (a) 444 sq. units
  • (b) 92\dfrac9229​ sq. units
  • (c) 72\dfrac7227​ sq. units
  • (d) 666 sq. units

The corner inputs are 000 and 111. Checking the three sign pieces gives intersections at x=−1,2x=-1,2x=−1,2. The upper curve is 3−∣x∣3-|x|3−∣x∣.

The vertical gap is

{2+2x,−1≤x≤0,2,0≤x≤1,4−2x,1≤x≤2.\begin{cases} 2+2x,&-1\le x\le0,\\ 2,&0\le x\le1,\\ 4-2x,&1\le x\le2. \end{cases}⎩⎨⎧​2+2x,2,4−2x,​−1≤x≤0,0≤x≤1,1≤x≤2.​

Hence A=1+2+1=4A=1+2+1=\boxed4A=1+2+1=4​, (a).

Another possible approach — change the view. The adjacent side vectors are AB→=(1,1)\overrightarrow{AB}=(1,1)AB=(1,1) and BC→=(2,−2)\overrightarrow{BC}=(2,-2)BC=(2,−2). Their dot product is 2−2=02-2=02−2=0, so the sides meet at right angles. The region is a rotated rectangle:

AB=2,BC=8=22,A=AB⋅BC=4.AB=\sqrt2,\quad BC=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2,\quad A=AB\cdot BC=4.AB=2​,BC=8​=22​,A=AB⋅BC=4.

The piecewise route is systematic; the rectangle view is faster once those perpendicular directions are noticed.

Coverage and source notes

All 252525 source questions appear in order: 181818 MCQs and 777 numerical questions. Independent calculations agree with the intended key. Q14's finite lower-envelope region and Q22's first positive intersection are explained before calculation. All area questions have actual local region diagrams.

The chapter covers vertical/horizontal strips, original domains and intersections, signed versus ordinary area, modulus and symmetry, geometric standard areas, trig/log/exponential regions, inequalities, equal-area parameters, circle segments/lenses and useful alternatives. Circle, ellipse, diamond and rectangle geometry preserves equal axis units.
